headline: One Wheel, Many Faiths: A Collage Artist Maps the Geometry of the Sacred
lede: Around 2021, a multimedia collage artist who goes by @policefala on X made an animated diagram — the product, she says, of sustained research — attempting to condense what she had found about a pattern shared by religious imagery across traditions. The work circulated for four years, losing her name along the way. In May 2025 she had to reclaim it from a repost account.
body:
The cached thumbnail from the animated GIF shows a medieval illuminated manuscript: a nine-armed spiral vortex set within a circular medallion, itself encircled by radiating golden sunbeams, with outstretched arms reaching in from either side. The composition is consistent with 12th- and 13th-century Rhineland mystical manuscripts — possibly from the tradition of Hildegard von Bingen, whose *Liber Divinorum Operum* features comparable spinning fire-wheels and cosmic-sphere visions. As a single frame, it is merely one exhibit; animated and sequenced against *sacred iconography* from other traditions, it becomes an argument: this visual grammar of **wheel, radiance, and center** recurs wherever human beings have tried to depict the divine.

The scholarly tradition behind such an argument runs deep. In *The Sacred and the Profane* (1959), **Mircea Eliade** documented the *axis mundi* — the cosmic pillar or world tree connecting underworld, earth, and heaven — appearing across Norse, Hindu, Amerindian, and Christian cosmologies without evidence of mutual borrowing. Carl Jung catalogued the *mandala* in *Mandala Symbolism* as a universal psychic form, arising spontaneously in Tibetan sand paintings, Navajo healing circles, Gothic rose windows, and psychiatric patients' drawings. Joseph Campbell, in *The Hero with a Thousand Faces* (1949), extended the convergence claim to narrative: his *monomyth* held that hero stories worldwide share a single deep structure — separation, initiation, return — and that visual symbols of radiance and center were expressions of the same underlying psychic reality.

Academic historians of religion today are considerably more cautious about these arguments. The Christian *nimbus* derives from Hellenistic portrayals of the sun god, borrowing prestige imagery from Roman imperial iconography; the Buddhist nimbus has a separate genealogy in South Asian conceptions of divine radiance (*tejas*). That both traditions depict their central figures surrounded by light tells us something about how religious art borrows prestige markers across cultural contact zones, not necessarily about a shared metaphysical substrate. The *Traditionalist School* — René Guénon and Frithjof Schuon, whose *The Transcendent Unity of Religions* (1948) T.S. Eliot called 'the most impressive work in the comparative study of Oriental and Occidental religion' — pushed the *philosophia perennis* claim furthest, arguing that identical symbols across traditions point to a single primordial metaphysical source. Most comparative religionists treat this as unfalsifiable theology in comparative method's clothing.

What Policefala's diagram adds to this long argument is the collage artist's move: not footnotes but juxtaposition, the visual analog to the scholarly comparative table. Her tags on related work — topology, alchemy, dyad, labyrinth, mitosis — suggest she was thinking about religious images as structurally equivalent under transformation, the way a topologist would say a doughnut and a coffee mug are the same shape. Whether the case holds depends on how strictly one defines 'structure,' and that question is precisely what the academic debate has never resolved. The diagram's persistence — circulating for four years, accumulating thousands of shares — suggests it resonates as a felt visual truth before any proof is demanded. That it traveled so far without its maker's name is a textbook case of *attribution decay*, the routine stripping of context from images as they move through social platforms.

concepts.definition: The visual imagery used in religious traditions to represent the divine — figures, symbols, geometric forms, and narrative scenes. Scholars study these images both as historical artifacts and as carriers of theological meaning, and compare them across traditions to find recurring structures.

Latin for 'world axis': a cosmological symbol, found across many independent cultures, of a vertical pillar, tree, or mountain connecting the underworld, the human world, and the heavens. Mircea Eliade identified it in Norse mythology (Yggdrasil), Hindu cosmology (Mount Meru), and the Christian cross, arguing it reflects a universal category of sacred spatial orientation.

A circular diagram with a central focal point and concentric or radial structure, used in Hindu and Buddhist practice as a map of the cosmos or an aid to meditation. Carl Jung argued the mandala is a universal psychological symbol that arises spontaneously across cultures as an expression of psychic wholeness, independent of religious transmission.

Joseph Campbell's term for the narrative structure he argued underlies all hero stories worldwide: departure from the ordinary world, initiation through ordeal, and return transformed. Influential in popular culture (George Lucas credited it for Star Wars) but contested by academic folklorists and mythologists who find the schema too loose to be falsifiable.

A halo or luminous aura surrounding the head — or, in some traditions, the entire body — of a divine or sanctified figure in religious art. Found across Christian, Buddhist, Hindu, and Zoroastrian iconographic traditions, though its theological meaning differs in each, and its historical transmission often followed trade and conquest routes rather than independent invention.

A Sanskrit term for divine radiance or luminous power, believed in Vedic and Hindu thought to emanate from gods, heroes, and accomplished ascetics. It underlies the South Asian artistic convention of depicting sacred figures surrounded by flames or golden light — the same visual idiom that the Christian nimbus and Buddhist prabha-mandala also express, albeit from different starting points.

A 20th-century intellectual movement, associated with René Guénon, Frithjof Schuon, and Ananda Coomaraswamy, that argued all world religions share a single esoteric core, the philosophia perennis, and that their doctrinal differences are surface variations on one primordial metaphysical truth. Influential in esotericism and some strands of comparative religion; regarded with skepticism by mainstream academic historians of religion.

Latin for 'perennial philosophy': the idea, associated with Leibniz and popularized in the 20th century by Aldous Huxley and the Traditionalist School, that a single universal truth underlies all major world religions. In its strongest form it claims that surface doctrinal differences are secondary to a shared metaphysical core; in its weakest, it simply notes recurring themes across independent religious developments.

The process by which images, writing, or other creative work loses its connection to its creator as it circulates on social media. Reposts, screenshots, and aggregator accounts routinely strip metadata and credit lines, so viral content often travels farther than it ever would have with the creator's name attached — while earning them nothing and making reclamation awkward.

books.title: The Sacred and the Profane: The Nature of Religion
books.author: Mircea Eliade
books.summary: Published in 1959, this is Eliade's most accessible statement of his phenomenological approach to comparative religion. It maps how sacred space (organized around the axis mundi), sacred time (ritual return to origins), and symbolic cosmology recur across independent traditions. Enormously influential in religious studies for two decades; later criticized for imposing universal structures at the expense of historical and cultural particularity.

books.title: Mandala Symbolism
books.author: C.G. Jung
books.summary: Extracted from Jung's Collected Works (vol. 9i), this text gathers his analysis of the mandala as a cross-cultural psychic symbol appearing in Tibetan Buddhism, medieval Christian alchemy, Navajo sand painting, and patients' spontaneous drawings. Jung argues the form emerges when the psyche seeks integration — which would explain why it arises independently across traditions rather than through transmission.

books.title: The Hero with a Thousand Faces
books.author: Joseph Campbell
books.summary: Published in 1949, this is the book that popularized the monomyth: the argument that hero narratives worldwide follow a single deep structural arc. Campbell synthesizes Frazer's comparative mythology, Jungian psychology, and van Gennep's rites-of-passage theory. Hugely influential on filmmakers and storytellers; contested by academic folklorists who find the schema too elastic to constitute genuine structural analysis.

books.title: The Transcendent Unity of Religions
books.author: Frithjof Schuon
books.summary: First published in French in 1948, this is the foundational text of the Traditionalist School. Schuon distinguishes the exoteric (outer, doctrinal) from the esoteric (inner, metaphysical) dimension of religion and argues that at the esoteric level all major religions converge on a single truth. T.S. Eliot called it 'the most impressive work in the comparative study of Oriental and Occidental religion'; most academic scholars of religion are more skeptical of its metaphysical premises.

fact_check: The animated GIF's full content could not be retrieved directly — X/Twitter requires authentication for media access, and only the video thumbnail was preserved in the bookmark application's cache. The brief's description of the diagram's visual argument is inferred from that thumbnail (which clearly shows a nine-armed vortex wheel within a solar nimbus, with outstretched hands) combined with the creator's own description and her documented interests. The identification of the thumbnail as possibly from the Hildegard von Bingen tradition is plausible but unconfirmed — similar imagery appears in several Rhineland mystical manuscripts. The specific image's source manuscript was not verified.
